prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the clearest case on the shortlist of a sharp theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) followed years later by an experimental discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, Jarillo-Herrero and co-workers, 2018) that created a new field. It gives a tunable, clean platform for strongly correlated electrons, and its influence now extends to fractional Chern insulators and other moire systems. As a statistical physicist I value that the work turned a many-body problem into something controllable by a single knob, the twist angle. Five of eight members ranked it in the top three, including members whose primary fields differ, which is better evidence of breadth than a single enthusiast. I rank it above my own opening first choice because the support for that choice proved to be mine alone.
statement.case_against: The mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved and the discovery dates only to 2018, so the committee may be early. Attribution is also not clean: first author Yuan Cao and other groups (Dean, Young, Kim, Yazdani) are outside the credited names, and earlier theory on twisted-bilayer band structure by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto predates Bistritzer-MacDonald. Naming Bistritzer as a third laureate adds a name that Eriksson-Olle and some others treat as joint with MacDonald, and this could look like padding the theory side.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first, arguing that the Z2 invariant changed what band theory can say, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene third with only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero credited.
responses.response: I accept that the Z2 classification is a conceptual advance and I do not dispute its maturity. My difficulty is attribution: the credited names (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan) leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose proposal preceded Molenkamp's measurement, and the three-name cap forces a split between the 2D and 3D parts that I cannot make fairly. Twisted bilayer graphene has a cleaner theory-plus-experiment split. On Bistritzer, I think the 2011 paper is genuinely joint, so I keep three names but would accept two if the committee prefers a compact citation.

responses.point: Olsson considers the twisted bilayer graphene discovery exceptional in impact but arguably early, because the superconducting mechanism is unsettled and the experiments date from 2018. She puts the lattice clock first.
responses.response: I take the maturity concern seriously and share it. But the prize is for the discovery of the phases and the prediction of the flat bands, not for the pairing mechanism, and both are reproduced by many groups. A mechanism that remains open is common for prizes in correlated matter. I would be more worried if the citation claimed an explanation of the superconductivity, so I keep the citation to prediction and discovery of the states.

responses.point: Lindroth and Kroll rank optical lattice clocks first, stressing the magic-wavelength concept and Ye's record systematic uncertainty, with the prospective redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that this is a clean two-person prize with a distinct contribution after the 2005 comb prize, and I keep it as my first alternative. I place it below moire matter because its impact is mostly on the measurement community and on tests that have so far not found anything, whereas moire matter has opened a new field of physics that others are actively building on. That is a judgement about breadth, not about quality, and the committee could reasonably reverse it.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, but notes that the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, so a second prize in the same family needs a distinct justification.
responses.response: I put circuit QED sixth because of exactly that timing issue, and because the credit among Yale and Zurich groups and Girvin would be hard to resolve with three names. His own candour about the overlap with 2025 matters more to me than the opening rank. I do not see the same difficulty with twisted bilayer graphene, which has no recent recognised prize in its family.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first with the same three names, relying on his recollection that the theory-plus-experiment split is natural, and acknowledges the Dean, Kim, Young and Yazdani groups are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the configuration and with the main concern. I would add that the outside groups, and Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, make the citation wording important: it should name the prediction and the discovery of the states, and not the broader twistronics field, so that omissions are easier to defend.

uncertainties: Whether three names or two is the right compact configuration, given how joint the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper is.
Whether the committee regards the unresolved superconducting mechanism as a reason to wait.
How to weigh my own opening first choice (condensates) against its lack of support and its position at the edge of physics.
Whether the credit omissions (Cao, Dean, Young, Kim, Yazdani, Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) are tolerable under the Nobel three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. His documented co-authors and positions do not include any credited name on the shortlist. His field (statistical physics of complex systems) is close to the biomolecular condensates candidate, but that is a field affinity and not a personal or institutional connection.
